title: How To Be Both Calm And Enthusiastic Next School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin addresses a question that frequently arises from his writing about calm teaching: how to reconcile calmness with enthusiasm. He explains that calm is an internal, all-day state of mind rather than an outward performance, meaning a teacher can act out a lively story while remaining internally relaxed. He then draws a distinction between enthusiasm and reserve, arguing enthusiasm should be reserved for directed teaching moments, where energy captures interest, while reserve — a quieter voice, minimal movement, slower pace — is better suited to giving directions and information, where it narrows student focus onto the task at hand. Linsin observes that many teachers get this reversed, becoming animated to coax compliance but flat and repetitive during actual instruction. Getting the balance right, he argues, produces happier students, less misbehavior, and more effective teaching overall.
points: Calmness is an internal, all-day disposition rather than an outward performance, meaning it's compatible with visibly enthusiastic teaching moments.
Enthusiasm and reserve should be deliberately deployed at different times: enthusiasm during directed lessons to capture interest, reserve during directions/information to narrow focus.
During directions, teachers should slow their breathing, limit movement, speak more softly, and provide only essential details.
Many teachers unintentionally reverse this pattern — becoming animated to coax compliance but flat and repetitive during actual instruction — undermining both engagement and clarity.
Getting the calm/enthusiasm balance right is presented as producing happier, less misbehaving students and significantly more effective teaching.
quotes: A calm disposition can sweep excitability right out of your classroom. It can improve listening and attentiveness. It can curb misbehavior and accelerate maturity.
Calmness, of the kind that permeates the classroom and rubs off on students, is more of an inward feeling than an outward appearance.
To be most effective, you'll want to save your enthusiasm for directed lessons.
But the moment you transition to giving directions or providing information, it’s best to draw down your energy.
They clap and exhort and bounce around the room trying to coax students into doing what they want, including behave, but then all but fall asleep during directed teaching.
It also demands that you know when to show enthusiasm and when to be reserved. Get these right, and your teaching will be infinitely more effective.
